soil-water-229.q: How did Veihmeyer and Hendrickson define readily available water?
soil-water-229.a: As the difference between the water content at field capacity and at the permanent wilting point.

soil-water-236.q: How can soil moisture sensors act like a thermostat for irrigation?
soil-water-236.a: They trigger irrigation only when soil moisture drops below a set depletion threshold.

soil-water-179.q: Why can the capillary fringe stay saturated much higher in some soils than others?
soil-water-179.a: Small, uniform pores can keep soil saturated several feet above the water table, while large pores limit the saturated part to a few inches.

soil-water-213.q: Why is groundwater recharge hard to quantify?
soil-water-213.a: Evaporation, transpiration and infiltration must first be measured or estimated to close the water balance.

soil-phys-137.q: Why does a pale soil stay cooler than a dark one?
soil-phys-137.a: Paler soils have a higher albedo, so they stay cooler than dark soils.

soil-phys-140.q: Why are soil moisture and soil thermal properties often measured together?
soil-phys-140.a: Thermal properties depend strongly on volumetric water content, so the two are closely linked.

soil-phys-159.q: What temperature conditions produce needle ice?
soil-phys-159.a: Soil above 0 °C under surface air below 0 °C, so water rises by capillary action and freezes onto the growing column.

soil-phys-155.q: Why are clean sands and gravels not frost susceptible?
soil-phys-155.a: Their pores are too open for capillary flow.

soil-phys-139.q: Why does wet soil warm more slowly than dry soil?
soil-phys-139.a: Water raises its specific heat, and evaporating water takes up a great deal of energy.

soil-phys-138.q: On a day when the surface is warmer than the soil below, which way does heat flow?
soil-phys-138.a: Into the soil, since heat flows against the temperature gradient.

soil-chem-076.q: Who is considered the father of soil chemistry?
soil-chem-076.a: J. Thomas Way, who ran many experiments on ion exchange in soils in the early 1870s.

soil-chem-104.q: What chemical change in iron accompanies the formation of goethite?
soil-chem-104.a: Ferrous iron, iron(II), is oxidized to ferric iron, iron(III).

soil-chem-088.a: Tight hydrogen bonding between its layers keeps water from entering.

soil-chem-077.q: Why does it matter to know the reactions a chemical undergoes once it reaches soil?
soil-chem-077.a: They can raise or lower its toxicity, so knowing them helps predict a contaminant's fate and design cost-effective clean-up.

soil-chem-083.q: Why do clay minerals feature in theories of the origin of life?
soil-chem-083.a: Montmorillonite has been shown to catalyse joining nucleotides into RNA and forming lipid membranes.

soil-chem-098.q: In what kind of soil is imogolite found?
soil-chem-098.a: In soils formed from volcanic ash.

soil-chem-110.q: How does palygorskite's structure differ from that of layered smectites?
soil-chem-110.a: It has a ribbon structure of continuous silica chains with long water channels inside, and it does not swell.

soil-chem-091.a: Its layers are not rigidly joined, so water and hydrated cations can enter the interlayer reversibly.

soil-chem-092.q: What happens to smectite in contact with potassium-rich groundwater?
soil-chem-092.a: Potassium replaces sodium and collapses the interlayer, turning it into non-swelling illite.

soil-chem-058.q: What three fractions make up humic substances, and how do they differ?
soil-chem-058.a: Humic acid, fulvic acid and humin, which differ in solubility.

soil-chem-073.q: How can leonardite help on metal-contaminated ground?
soil-chem-073.a: Added to the soil, especially with compost, it reduces the uptake of metals by plants.

soil-chem-072.q: Why do micronutrient fertilizers need a chelating agent such as EDTA?
soil-chem-072.a: Without one, the phosphate salts in most fertilizers turn the metal ions into insoluble solids of no use to plants.
